question: Does feeding many GPUs to the block-tridiagonal Newton solve shorten its depth from T ordered steps to log2(T)?
hypothesis: Parallel cyclic reduction solves the tridiagonal Newton correction in log2(T) rounds instead of T, so GPU width shortens the sequential part [s3].

compute_axis.quantity: number of equations (time steps) in one tridiagonal Newton correction

held_fixed: matrix structure: diagonally dominant tridiagonal, unit-magnitude off-diagonals, diagonal dominance margin 1.0
GPU: A100 SXM 40GB (108 SMs, 6912 FP32 cores)
5 timing repeats per (solver, N), median reported

predictions.if_lever: As equation count N grows, cyclic-reduction wall-clock grows like log2(N) and beats the sequential Thomas solve by a widening margin.
predictions.if_not: At feasible N the parallel solver never beats sequential: extra work and memory traffic dominate, and one GPU has too few threads to hide them.
predictions.decision_rule: Lever if median PCR time < median Thomas time at n_max=2^24 by at least gate_speedup=2x, and the PCR/Thomas speedup grows with N; otherwise not.
predictions.noise_rule: Five repeats per (solver, N) on one A100; report median and interquartile range; a real difference is a speedup whose lower quartile still exceeds 1 (and 2 at n_max).
predictions.expected_why: Cyclic reduction's logarithmic depth is textbook and Zhang et al. already measured large GPU speedups over sequential tridiagonal solves [s2].

compute_tested_why: The test varies N, the system size, and measures whether the parallel PCR solver's depth grows as log2(N) while sequential Thomas grows as N, which is exactly the depth reduction more parallel compute is claimed to buy.
scored_against: Both solvers are scored against cuSPARSE gtsv2_nopivot and scipy.linalg.solve_banded (relative residual < 1e-10); the speedup decision compares PCR wall-clock to Thomas wall-clock on the same A100.

arms.what: Thomas: sequential forward elimination + back substitution (baseline_sequential)
PCR: parallel cyclic reduction, log2(N) rounds (method under test)
cuSPARSE gtsv2_nopivot: NVIDIA hybrid PCR+Thomas (independent reference)
Batched Thomas: K independent systems solved concurrently (baseline_copies)

baseline.what: Thomas algorithm, O(N) sequential forward elimination and back substitution [s1], timed as a hand-written CUDA kernel on the same A100

anchor.what: Written PCR and Thomas kernels must match NVIDIA's gtsv tridiagonal solve and a CPU dense solve to 1e-10 relative residual.
anchor.independent_code: cuSPARSE gtsv2_nopivot (GPU) and scipy.linalg.solve_banded (CPU) on the same diagonally dominant systems

checks: Thomas residual vs cuSPARSE gtsv2_nopivot < 1e-10 on diagonally dominant systems.
PCR residual vs cuSPARSE gtsv2_nopivot < 1e-10 on diagonally dominant systems.
PCR and Thomas solutions agree with scipy solve_banded to < 1e-8 relative.
cuSPARSE gtsv2_nopivot matches scipy solve_banded to < 1e-8 (validates the library reference).
PCR wall-clock grows ~ log2(N): flat per-doubling slope; Thomas slope ~2x per doubling.
Batched Thomas shows K copies at once raise throughput but do not lower one system's latency.

phases.what: Write CUDA Thomas, PCR and batched-Thomas kernels plus the timing harness locally (no GPU); port from pilot/pcr_thomas_check.py.
phases.stop_rule: Harness compiles with nvcc and builds against CUDA + cuSPARSE.

phases.what: On 1x A100 40GB: compile, then check Thomas and PCR against cuSPARSE gtsv2_nopivot and scipy solve_banded on diagonally dominant systems at N=2^10 and 2^14.
phases.stop_rule: Max relative residual reported for both solvers.

gate.else: Fix the kernels and re-run the anchor before starting the sweep.

phases.what: Sweep N over {2^10, 2^14, 2^18, 2^22, 2^24}; 5 repeats each; median wall-clock of Thomas, PCR, batched Thomas and cuSPARSE gtsv2_nopivot.
phases.stop_rule: All levels x solvers x 5 repeats recorded; speedup curve saved.

phases.what: Stretch: block-tridiagonal (block size d=4,16) PCR vs block Thomas, mirroring the block-bidiagonal Newton Jacobian.
phases.stop_rule: Block sweep recorded or time box ended.

phases.what: Stretch: PCR split across 2 and 8 A100 40GB GPUs to test further depth reduction.
phases.stop_rule: Multi-GPU timings recorded or time box ended.

restructuring.sequential_part: The block-bidiagonal Newton correction is a forward substitution: each row waits on the previous, T ordered steps.
restructuring.method: Cyclic reduction halves the system each round and solves independent rows together, so log2(T) rounds replace T ordered steps [s3].
restructuring.condition: The matrix must be diagonally dominant (Thomas/PCR-stable, no zero pivots), and the GPU must keep enough threads in flight to hide the log2(T) rounds' memory latency rather than serialise them; check the residual in p1_anchor and compare the known thread count (108 SMs, 6912 cores [s4]) against N.
restructuring.baseline_sequential: Hand-written CUDA Thomas kernel (forward elimination then back substitution, one thread per system), tuned with a register-cached recurrence and #pragma unroll; also timed against MKL dgtsv on the instance CPU as a floor.
restructuring.baseline_copies: Batched Thomas: K independent diagonally dominant systems solved concurrently (one thread block per system) at the same N, showing width raises throughput while one system's latency stays O(N).

scope_gap: The full parallel-in-time Newton loop: this plan times the tridiagonal solve alone, not the k-iteration Parareal/MGRIT correction whose count the forgetting rate sets.
Block-bidiagonal multiple-shooting Jacobians with state dimension d>16, and how block size changes PCR's advantage.

novelty.closest_prior: Zhang, Cohen and Owens benchmarked cyclic reduction, PCR and recursive doubling on a GTX 280, finding PCR does fewer steps, more work, and 28x over sequential LAPACK [s2].
novelty.left_open: No published result times PCR against an on-GPU sequential Thomas on a modern A100 across N up to 2^24, so the crossover is unmeasured.

limits: Shows one tridiagonal solve's wall-clock scaling on one modern GPU, not the end-to-end parallel-in-time method, whose iteration count the dynamics sets.
test_summary: Time a sequential Thomas tridiagonal solve against parallel cyclic reduction on one A100, sweeping N=2^10 to 2^24, checking both match NVIDIA's gtsv reference and batched independent solves.

sources.quote: For such systems, the solution can be obtained in O(n) operations instead of O(n^3) required by Gaussian elimination.
sources.supports: Thomas algorithm is O(N) work and inherently one-at-a-time (forward sweep then back substitution) — the sequential baseline.

sources.quote: We find that CR enjoys linear algorithm complexity but suffers from more algorithmic steps and bank conflicts, while PCR and RD have fewer algorithmic steps but do more work each step.
sources.supports: PCR has fewer (logarithmic) steps but more work per step; the prior GPU benchmark and the 28x speedup proxy.

sources.quote: The Thomas algorithm, based on LU decomposition, is efficient to solve tridiagonal systems but inherently sequential, while the PCR algorithm is more computationally expensive but parallelizable. The hybrid combination of the two algorithms is used to achieve the best performance for different problem sizes.
sources.supports: Thomas is sequential and PCR is parallel (the depth claim); NVIDIA ships a PCR+Thomas hybrid, used as the independent reference.
